The test image shows a corn ear with dense white/gray fluffy mold covering a central section of kernels, with some greenish patches visible within the mold mass. Healthy yellow kernels are visible on either side. This points toward an ear rot.

Key observations:
- Predominantly white to light gray, cottony/fluffy mold
- Some greenish patches within the mold
- Covers a section of the ear (not clearly tip or base)
- Dense mycelial growth over kernels

Top candidates: **Ear_rots_Diplodia** (white mold becoming grayish-brown) or **Ear_rots_Trichoderma** (dark green). Let me check the Diplodia reference.

The reference images for Diplodia show dried, grayish-brown, chalky kernels in a late stage. The test image shows much more active, fluffy white mold with some greenish areas — this matches early-to-mid stage Diplodia ear rot (the white mold phase before it dries and turns grayish-brown). The description explicitly states "white mold beginning at the base of the ear that becomes grayish-brown."

The green patches could indicate secondary colonization or early Diplodia transitioning. The dense, white, cottony mycelial growth over corn kernels is the hallmark early presentation of Diplodia, distinct from:
- Gibberella (pink/red mold from tip)
- Fusarium (salmon/pink with starburst pattern)
- Trichoderma (distinctly dark green)
- Aspergillus (olive-green powdery, usually at tip)
